issues.legal_issue: A statutory right of pre-emption over immovable property does not accrue from an agreement to sell before a valid sale is completed by the required registered conveyance.
material_facts: The pre-emption suit was filed on the basis of agreements to sell agricultural land.
The sale deed for the disputed land was executed only after the suit was filed.
The court treated the agreements as creating no interest in the land and found that no sale had been completed when the suit was brought.
issues.conclusion: No enforceable right of pre-emption had accrued when the suit was filed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 176 and 183 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, a right of pre-emption could arise on a qualifying transfer. But where the Transfer of Property Act applied, section 54 required a registered instrument to transfer ownership of immovable property of the relevant value, and a contract for sale did not itself create an interest in the property. Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act reinforced the need for registration. The court distinguished the broader approach to identifying a sale under Mohammedan law in Begum v. Mohammad Yakub and considered Sitaram Bhaurao Deshmukh v. Jiaul Hasan Sirajul Khan, Immudipattam Thirugnana S. O. Kondema Naik v. Peria Dorasami, and the reasoning in Janki v. Girjadat concerning the need for a valid and perfected sale before pre-emption could be exercised.

predicates.preemption_suit: A claimant brings a proceeding seeking to exercise a right of pre-emption over a property transfer.
predicates.registered_conveyance_required: The relevant transfer of immovable property requires a registered conveyance to pass ownership.
predicates.no_registered_sale_at_filing: No registered instrument completing the sale existed when the pre-emption proceeding was brought.
predicates.preemption_right_not_accrued: The claimant's right to enforce pre-emption had not yet arisen.

issues.definition: When a pre-emption proceeding is brought before a required registered conveyance has completed the sale, the right to enforce pre-emption has not yet arisen.

issues.legal_issue: Using lawful means to avoid the accrual of a statutory right of pre-emption is not, without more, fraudulent.
material_facts: The appellant and vendors had made agreements to sell before executing a registered sale deed.
The sale was not completed until the sale deed was executed.
The court found no basis to treat the parties' pre-deed conduct as fraud merely because it avoided the accrual of a pre-emption right.
issues.conclusion: The parties' use of lawful means to avoid a pre-emption claim did not amount to fraud.
issues.legal_principle: The right of pre-emption is a weak right and is not viewed with favour by courts; it may be defeated by legitimate methods. The court relied on Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh and held that it is neither illegal nor fraudulent for parties to avoid a pre-emption claim by lawful means. Conduct before a pre-emptible transfer is completed does not, merely because it prevents the right from arising, constitute fraud.

predicates.preemption_claim: A claimant seeks to exercise a right of pre-emption over a proposed or completed transfer.
predicates.parties_used_lawful_means: The transferor and transferee arranged or completed their dealings using lawful means.
predicates.no_unlawful_conduct_shown: The record does not establish unlawful conduct beyond the parties' effort to avoid a pre-emption claim.
predicates.lawful_avoidance_not_fraudulent: The parties' lawful effort to avoid the pre-emption claim is not fraudulent.

issues.definition: Where parties use lawful means and no unlawful conduct is shown, their effort to avoid a pre-emption claim is not fraudulent.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption suit founded on an agreement to sell cannot be sustained by a later sale when the claimant did not base the suit on that later sale.
material_facts: The claimant filed suit before the sale deed was executed and founded the claim on earlier agreements to sell.
The registered sale deed was executed after the suit was filed.
The claimant did not base the suit on the later completed sale.
issues.conclusion: The suit as pleaded could not be maintained as a claim to pre-empt the later sale.
issues.legal_principle: A pre-emption claim must rest on a pre-emptible transfer that has occurred. The court held that the claimant had sued to pre-empt the earlier agreements, which did not transfer ownership, and did not sue on the later sale. It also noted that, had the claimant relied on the later sale, the appellant could have raised defences relevant to that transfer. The court would not go out of its way to assist a pre-emptor, given the weak nature of the right.

predicates.preemption_suit: A claimant brings a proceeding seeking to pre-empt a property transfer.
predicates.claim_based_on_sale_agreement: The claimant bases the pre-emption claim on an agreement to sell rather than a completed sale.
predicates.later_sale_not_basis_of_claim: A sale is completed later, but the claimant does not rely on that later sale as the basis of the suit.
predicates.suit_on_agreement_not_maintainable_as_cl: The suit founded on the agreement cannot be treated as a maintainable claim to pre-empt the later sale.

issues.definition: If a claimant bases a pre-emption suit on an agreement to sell and does not rely on a later completed sale, the suit cannot be maintained as a claim on that later sale.
